title: Workouts
text:
Show code
source("R/load_data.R")
library(patchwork)
With 269 swimming sessions out of 364 total workouts, swimming defines the training load. This page breaks down workout patterns — when you swim, how hard, and how it relates to recovery.

title: Workouts
text:
Activity breakdown


Show code
workouts |>
  count(activity_grp) |>
  mutate(activity_grp = fct_reorder(activity_grp, n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = activity_grp, fill = activity_grp)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85, width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = -0.3, size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    Swimming = "#3266ad", Lifting = "#1D9E75", Running = "#BA7517",
    Basketball = "#7F77DD", Other = "#888780"
  )) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(title = "Total sessions by activity", x = "Sessions", y = NULL) +
  theme_whoop() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")





Total sessions by activity type across the 13-month period.

title: Workouts
section: Workout timing: when do you train?
text:
Workout timing: when do you train?
The FDA textbook plots circadian patterns in NHANES accelerometry data; here we apply the same idea to workout start times — showing when each activity tends to occur throughout the day.


Show code
workouts |>
  filter(activity_grp %in% c("Swimming", "Lifting"), !is.na(workout_hour)) |>
  count(activity_grp, workout_hour) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = workout_hour, y = n, fill = activity_grp)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", alpha = 0.85, width = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Swimming = "#3266ad", Lifting = "#1D9E75"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(0, 5, 6, 9, 12, 15, 17, 20),
    labels = c("12am", "5am", "6am", "9am", "12pm", "3pm", "5pm", "8pm")
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Workout start time by activity",
    subtitle = "Swimming peaks at 5am and 3pm; weightlifting at 5pm",
    x = "Hour of day", y = "Sessions"
  ) +
  theme_whoop()





Session count by hour of day for Swimming and Weightlifting. Swimming shows two clear peaks: early morning (~5am) and afternoon (~3pm). Weightlifting is almost exclusively an evening (5pm) activity.

title: Workouts
text:
Swimming: monthly volume


Show code
workouts |>
  filter(activity_grp == "Swimming") |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarise(
    sessions     = n(),
    avg_duration = mean(duration_min, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = sessions * 5), fill = "#3266ad", alpha = 0.3, width = 25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = avg_duration), color = "#3266ad", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = avg_duration), color = "#3266ad", size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 months", date_labels = "%b '%y") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Avg duration (min)",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . / 5, name = "Sessions (bars)")
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Monthly swimming volume",
    subtitle = "Bars = session count (right axis) · Line = avg duration (left axis)",
    x = NULL
  ) +
  theme_whoop()





Monthly swimming session count and average duration. Duration is fairly stable (~95–105 min/session) while volume peaks in spring-summer 2023.

title: Workouts
text:
Heart rate zones during swimming
HR zone time reveals training intensity distribution. Zone 2 (aerobic base) and Zone 3 (tempo) dominate, with intermittent Zone 4–5 work.


Show code
workouts |>
  filter(activity_grp == "Swimming", !is.na(z1)) |>
  summarise(
    `Zone 1` = mean(z1, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Zone 2` = mean(z2, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Zone 3` = mean(z3, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Zone 4` = mean(z4, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Zone 5` = mean(z5, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "zone", values_to = "pct") |>
  mutate(zone = factor(zone, levels = paste("Zone", 1:5))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = zone, y = pct, fill = zone)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85, width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(pct), "%")), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Zone 1" = "#B5D4F4", "Zone 2" = "#3266ad",
    "Zone 3" = "#1D9E75", "Zone 4" = "#BA7517", "Zone 5" = "#E24B4A"
  )) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(
    title    = "Average HR zone distribution — swimming",
    subtitle = "Percentage of session time in each zone",
    x = NULL, y = "% of session time"
  ) +
  theme_whoop() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")





Average percentage of swimming session time spent in each HR zone. Zone 1 = very light, Zone 5 = maximal effort.

title: Workouts
text:
Strain vs. same-day recovery
Like the CD4 scatter in the FDA textbook, this plot treats each workout as a functional observation and asks: does recovery predict how hard you train?


Show code
swim_data <- workouts |>
  filter(activity_grp == "Swimming", !is.na(w_strain), !is.na(recovery))

swim_cor <- cor(swim_data$recovery, swim_data$w_strain, use = "complete.obs") |> round(3)

ggplot(swim_data, aes(x = recovery, y = w_strain, color = rec_zone,
                       size = duration_min)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, shape = 16) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#111", linewidth = 0.8,
              fill = "grey85", alpha = 0.4, inherit.aes = FALSE,
              aes(x = recovery, y = w_strain)) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(Green = "#1D9E75", Yellow = "#BA7517", Red = "#E24B4A"),
    name = "Recovery zone"
  ) +
  scale_size_continuous(name = "Duration (min)", range = c(1.5, 6), breaks = c(60, 90, 120)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Swim session strain vs. same-day recovery",
    subtitle = paste0("Pearson r = ", swim_cor, " — nearly zero correlation"),
    x = "Recovery score (%)", y = "Session strain"
  ) +
  theme_whoop()





Each point is a swimming session. X-axis: same-day recovery score. Y-axis: session strain. Point size encodes duration. Color encodes recovery zone. The near-zero correlation suggests you trained at consistent intensity regardless of readiness.










Note



r = 0.022 — essentially no relationship between how recovered you were and how hard you swam. This is common in competitive swimmers who follow structured training programs and push through regardless of readiness signals.

title: Workouts
text:
Session strain distribution


Show code
workouts |>
  filter(!is.na(w_strain)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = w_strain, fill = activity_grp)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, color = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    Swimming = "#3266ad", Lifting = "#1D9E75", Running = "#BA7517",
    Basketball = "#7F77DD", Other = "#888780"
  ), name = "Activity") +
  labs(
    title    = "Workout strain distribution",
    subtitle = "WHOOP strain score (0–21 scale)",
    x = "Session strain", y = "Sessions"
  ) +
  theme_whoop()

title: WHOOP Biometrics · Personal Dashboard
text:
Show code
source("R/load_data.R")
library(patchwork)
library(ggridges)
This site explores a year-plus of personal data from the WHOOP wearable, applying exploratory analysis techniques inspired by the Functional Data Analysis with R textbook. Each daily measurement is treated as a sample from an underlying physiological process — the goal is to visualize longitudinal patterns, identify structure, and surface insights that the WHOOP app alone doesn’t show.

title: WHOOP Biometrics · Personal Dashboard
text:
Recovery over time
The plot below shows daily recovery scores with a 7-day rolling mean smoothing out day-to-day noise — analogous to the functional mean estimators in Chapter 1 of the FDA textbook.


Show code
ggplot(cycles, aes(x = date)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = recovery, color = rec_zone), alpha = 0.45, size = 1.2, shape = 16) +
  geom_line(aes(y = recovery_7), color = "#111111", linewidth = 0.9, na.rm = TRUE) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(Green = "#1D9E75", Yellow = "#BA7517", Red = "#E24B4A"),
    name = "Zone"
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 months", date_labels = "%b '%y") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100), breaks = c(0, 33, 67, 100)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(34, 67), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey70", linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(
    title    = "Daily recovery score",
    subtitle = "7-day rolling mean overlaid in black",
    x = NULL, y = "Recovery (%)"
  ) +
  theme_whoop()





Daily recovery (points) with 7-day rolling mean (line). Color encodes WHOOP recovery zones: green ≥ 67%, yellow 34–66%, red < 34%.

title: Recovery & HRV
text:
Show code
source("R/load_data.R")
library(patchwork)
HRV — the millisecond variation between heartbeats — is the closest non-invasive proxy for autonomic nervous system readiness. Higher HRV generally signals better recovery; lower HRV reflects accumulated stress, illness, or overtraining. WHOOP measures it each morning during a brief calibration window.

title: Recovery & HRV
text:
HRV over time


Show code
# IQR reference band
hrv_q <- quantile(cycles$hrv, probs = c(0.25, 0.75), na.rm = TRUE)

ggplot(cycles, aes(x = date)) +
  annotate("rect",
    xmin = min(cycles$date), xmax = max(cycles$date),
    ymin = hrv_q[1], ymax = hrv_q[2],
    fill = "#3266ad", alpha = 0.07
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(y = hrv, color = rec_zone), alpha = 0.4, size = 1.3, shape = 16) +
  geom_line(aes(y = hrv_7), color = "#3266ad", linewidth = 1, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = avg_hrv, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey50") +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(Green = "#1D9E75", Yellow = "#BA7517", Red = "#E24B4A"),
    name = "Recovery zone"
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 months", date_labels = "%b '%y") +
  annotate("text", x = min(cycles$date) + 5, y = avg_hrv + 4,
           label = paste0("Mean = ", avg_hrv, " ms"), size = 3, color = "grey50") +
  labs(
    title    = "Heart rate variability (HRV)",
    subtitle = "Blue band = interquartile range · Dotted line = overall mean",
    x = NULL, y = "HRV (ms)"
  ) +
  theme_whoop()





Daily HRV (points) and 7-day rolling mean (line). Colored bands mark the interquartile range across the full period. Notable: the July 2023 RHR/HRV anomaly is visible as several days of very low HRV coinciding with an RHR spike to 120 bpm — likely illness or injury.

title: Recovery & HRV
text:
HRV vs. Resting Heart Rate
RHR and HRV should move in opposite directions under healthy adaptation — high HRV paired with low RHR is the ideal combination. The scatter below shows this inverse relationship in your data.


Show code
cycles |>
  filter(!is.na(hrv), !is.na(rhr), rhr < 80) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rhr, y = hrv, color = rec_zone)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.8, shape = 16) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#111", linewidth = 0.8,
              fill = "grey85", alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(Green = "#1D9E75", Yellow = "#BA7517", Red = "#E24B4A"),
    name = "Recovery zone"
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "HRV vs. resting heart rate",
    subtitle = "Linear trend with 95% confidence band",
    x = "Resting heart rate (bpm)", y = "HRV (ms)"
  ) +
  theme_whoop()





Each point is one day. The negative correlation between HRV and RHR is clearly visible; outliers in the top-right corner (high HRV and high RHR) typically coincide with illness events. Points filtered to RHR < 80 to exclude sensor artifacts.






Show code
cor_val <- cor(cycles$hrv, cycles$rhr, use = "complete.obs") |> round(3)



The Pearson correlation between daily HRV and RHR is r = -0.177, confirming the expected inverse relationship.

title: Recovery & HRV
section: Rolling means: HRV, RHR, and Strain
text:
Rolling means: HRV, RHR, and Strain
This three-panel view (modeled after the NHANES multi-panel plots in the FDA textbook) shows 7-day rolling means for all three key recovery metrics simultaneously, making it easier to spot periods where all three converged or diverged.


Show code
illness_bands <- tibble(
  xmin = as_date(c("2023-04-03", "2023-07-26")),
  xmax = as_date(c("2023-04-15", "2023-07-31"))
)

make_band <- function(p) {
  p + geom_rect(
    data = illness_bands,
    aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
    fill = "#E24B4A", alpha = 0.08, inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 months", date_labels = "%b '%y") +
  theme_whoop() +
  labs(x = NULL)
}

p1 <- ggplot(cycles, aes(x = date, y = hrv_7)) +
  geom_line(color = "#3266ad", linewidth = 0.9, na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "HRV — 7-day rolling mean", y = "ms")

p2 <- ggplot(cycles, aes(x = date, y = rhr_7)) +
  geom_line(color = "#E24B4A", linewidth = 0.9, na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "Resting heart rate — 7-day rolling mean", y = "bpm")

p3 <- ggplot(cycles, aes(x = date, y = strain_7)) +
  geom_line(color = "#BA7517", linewidth = 0.9, na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "Day strain — 7-day rolling mean", y = "strain score")

make_band(p1) / make_band(p2) / make_band(p3)





7-day rolling averages for HRV, RHR, and day strain. Shaded regions highlight the two major illness/anomaly events (early April 2023 and late July 2023).










Note



Red shaded regions mark two anomalous periods: early April 2023 (recovery crashed to 1% on consecutive days, HRV dropped sharply) and late July 2023 (RHR spiked to 120 bpm for several days — almost certainly illness or an injury event).

title: Recovery & HRV
text:
Day-of-week patterns


Show code
cycles |>
  filter(!is.na(hrv)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = day_of_week, y = hrv, fill = day_of_week)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.size = 1, outlier.alpha = 0.4, width = 0.6) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.2, size = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = rep(c("#3266ad","#1D9E75","#BA7517","#E24B4A",
                                    "#7F77DD","#888780","#3266ad"), 1)) +
  labs(
    title    = "HRV by day of week",
    subtitle = "Boxplot with jittered raw values overlaid",
    x = NULL, y = "HRV (ms)"
  ) +
  theme_whoop() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")





Distribution of HRV by day of week. Sunday typically shows the highest HRV (post-rest), while mid-week shows more variability from accumulated training load.

title: Recovery & HRV
text:
Recovery score distribution


Show code
cycles |>
  ggplot(aes(x = recovery, fill = rec_zone)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = avg_recovery, linetype = "dashed", color = "#111") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(Green = "#1D9E75", Yellow = "#BA7517", Red = "#E24B4A"),
    name = "Zone"
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = avg_recovery + 2, y = 30, label = paste0("Mean = ", avg_recovery, "%"),
           size = 3.2, hjust = 0, color = "#111") +
  labs(
    title = "Recovery score distribution",
    subtitle = "Across all tracked days",
    x = "Recovery (%)", y = "Days"
  ) +

title: Sleep
text:
Show code
source("R/load_data.R")
library(patchwork)
library(tidyr)
Sleep architecture — the nightly mix of light, deep (slow-wave), and REM sleep — reflects both physiological need and recovery quality. The analyses here treat each night as a functional observation and look at how the composition changed over time.

title: Sleep
text:
Monthly sleep stage composition
Modeled after the COVID mortality composition plots in the FDA textbook, this stacked bar chart shows how average nightly sleep stage proportions shifted month to month.


Show code
monthly_sleep |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(light_avg, deep_avg, rem_avg, awake_avg),
               names_to = "stage", values_to = "minutes") |>
  mutate(
    stage = recode(stage,
      light_avg = "Light", deep_avg = "Deep (SWS)",
      rem_avg   = "REM",   awake_avg = "Awake"
    ) |> factor(levels = c("Light", "Deep (SWS)", "REM", "Awake"))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = minutes, fill = stage)) +
  geom_col(width = 25, color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Light"       = "#B5D4F4",
      "Deep (SWS)"  = "#3266ad",
      "REM"         = "#1D9E75",
      "Awake"       = "#D3D1C7"
    ),
    name = "Stage"
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 months", date_labels = "%b '%y") +
  labs(
    title    = "Monthly average sleep stage composition",
    subtitle = "Average minutes per stage per night (main sleeps only)",
    x = NULL, y = "Minutes per night"
  ) +
  theme_whoop()





Average nightly minutes per sleep stage, stacked by month. Only main overnight sleeps are included (naps excluded). Note the higher awake time in winter months and the drop in all stages in March–April 2024, which reflects fewer tracked nights in those months.

title: Sleep
section: Deep sleep and REM over time

title: Sleep
text:
Sleep efficiency distribution
Sleep efficiency = asleep time / time in bed. Values above 85% are generally considered good.


Show code
main_sleeps |>
  filter(!is.na(sleep_eff)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sleep_eff)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 3, fill = "#3266ad", color = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 85, linetype = "dashed", color = "#E24B4A", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 87, y = 40, label = "85% threshold",
           color = "#E24B4A", size = 3.2, hjust = 0) +
  labs(
    title    = "Sleep efficiency distribution",
    subtitle = "Percentage of time in bed actually asleep",
    x = "Sleep efficiency (%)", y = "Nights"
  ) +
  theme_whoop()





Distribution of sleep efficiency across all nights. The dashed line marks the 85% clinical threshold.

title: Sleep
text:
Sleep debt trajectory
WHOOP tracks cumulative sleep debt — how many minutes short of your sleep need you are. Sustained debt is associated with impaired recovery and performance.


Show code
main_sleeps |>
  filter(!is.na(sleep_debt)) |>
  arrange(date) |>
  mutate(
    debt_roll   = rollmean(sleep_debt, 7, fill = NA, align = "right", na.rm = TRUE),
    debt_zone   = case_when(
      sleep_debt <= 30  ~ "Low",
      sleep_debt <= 90  ~ "Moderate",
      TRUE              ~ "High"
    ) |> factor(levels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High"))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = sleep_debt, color = debt_zone), alpha = 0.35, size = 1.1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = debt_roll), color = "#111", linewidth = 0.9, na.rm = TRUE) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(Low = "#1D9E75", Moderate = "#BA7517", High = "#E24B4A"),
    name = "Debt level"
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 months", date_labels = "%b '%y") +
  labs(
    title    = "Sleep debt over time",
    subtitle = "Minutes below nightly sleep need · 7-day rolling mean in black",
    x = NULL, y = "Sleep debt (min)"
  ) +
  theme_whoop()





Daily sleep debt (points, colored by magnitude) with 7-day rolling mean. Peaks in debt often correspond to low-recovery periods seen in the Recovery page.

title: Sleep
text:
Sleep performance vs. next-day recovery
Does better sleep tonight predict better recovery tomorrow? We join sleep performance to the following day’s recovery score.


Show code
sleep_lag <- main_sleeps |>
  filter(!is.na(sleep_perf)) |>
  select(date, sleep_perf) |>
  mutate(next_date = date + 1) |>
  left_join(cycles |> select(date, recovery, rec_zone), by = c("next_date" = "date")) |>
  filter(!is.na(recovery))

sleep_lag_cor <- cor(sleep_lag$sleep_perf, sleep_lag$recovery, use = "complete.obs") |> round(3)

ggplot(sleep_lag, aes(x = sleep_perf, y = recovery, color = rec_zone)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 1.8, shape = 16) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#111", linewidth = 0.8,
              fill = "grey85", alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(Green = "#1D9E75", Yellow = "#BA7517", Red = "#E24B4A"),
    name = "Next-day zone"
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Sleep performance → next-day recovery",
    subtitle = paste0("Pearson r = ", sleep_lag_cor),
    x = "Sleep performance (%)", y = "Next-day recovery (%)"
  ) +
  theme_whoop()





Sleep performance (%) on the x-axis vs. next-day recovery score on the y-axis. Each point is one night. The positive trend suggests sleep quality does predict next-day readiness, but with substantial scatter — recovery is multifactorial.





r = 0.191 — a modest positive correlation. Sleep quality is one of the strongest predictors of next-day recovery among the variables tracked here.

title: Methods & Data Notes
text:
Show code
source("R/load_data.R")
library(dplyr)

title: Methods & Data Notes
text:
Data source
All data come from the WHOOP 4.0 wearable worn continuously from March 02, 2023 through April 02, 2024. Three CSV exports were used:








File
Content
Rows




physiological_cycles.csv
Daily recovery, HRV, RHR, strain, and embedded sleep summary
342


sleeps.csv
Individual sleep sessions including naps, with stage breakdown
370


workouts.csv
Individual workout sessions with HR zones and strain
364



Data were exported directly from the WHOOP app under Account → My Data → Export.

title: Methods & Data Notes
text:
Processing decisions
Physiological cycles. Rows with missing Recovery score % were dropped (25 rows removed). Rows where RHR > 80 bpm appear in the raw data from a known multi-day anomaly period (late July 2023) and are retained in the dataset but filtered out of correlation plots where noted.
Sleeps. The sleeps.csv file includes both overnight sleeps and naps (flagged via the Nap column). Naps are excluded from stage composition and sleep debt analyses but included in session counts.
Workouts. Activity names were consolidated from 11 distinct labels into 5 groups (Swimming, Lifting, Running, Basketball, Other). The Strength Trainer label was merged into Lifting.
Rolling means. All 7-day rolling averages use zoo::rollmean() with align = "right" and na.rm = TRUE, meaning the value at day t reflects the mean of the current and previous 6 days with available data. The 28-day rolling means on the sleep page use the same approach.

title: Methods & Data Notes
text:
Analytical inspiration
This project is modeled on the exploratory visualization approach in:

Goldsmith, J., Scheipl, F., Huang, L., Wrobel, J., Di, C., Gellar, J., … & Crainiceanu, C. (2024). Functional Data Analysis with R. Chapman & Hall / CRC.

Specific techniques borrowed: - Spaghetti + mean overlay (Chapter 1 CD4 example) → Recovery & HRV page - Stacked composition charts (COVID mortality page) → Sleep stage composition - Circadian timing plots (NHANES MIMS page) → Workout timing analysis - Scatter with smooth (CD4 individual trajectory plots) → Strain vs. recovery scatter

title: Methods & Data Notes
text:
Rendering this site
This is a Quarto website rendered with quarto render and deployed via GitHub Pages from the docs/ folder.
R packages required:
install.packages(c(
  "tidyverse",
  "lubridate",
  "zoo",
  "patchwork",
  "ggridges",
  "glue",
  "htmltools",
  "scales"
))
To render locally:
# From the project root
quarto render

# Or preview with live reload
quarto preview

title: Methods & Data Notes
text:
Known limitations

WHOOP’s HRV measurement uses a 5-minute morning calibration window, which can be sensitive to movement or breathing irregularities — single-day outliers should not be over-interpreted.
The sensor was removed during the late July 2023 anomaly period (RHR showing 120 bpm is a known artifact when the band is off but still recording).
Sleep stage classification is proprietary and not validated against polysomnography.
Workout start times are rounded to the hour in the export format.
